findings.truth: The spec cites the Ten Commandments as Exodus 20:2-14, the Jewish versification. Exodus 20:1-17 is the Christian numbering. Not mark-affecting, so no edit, but the spec's own citation is the one a student should quote.
findings.evidence: spec line 3186 'Importance of the Ten Commandments: Exodus 20:2-14'

findings.claim: The philosopher Abraham Joshua Heschel described the Sabbath as a “cathedral in time”
findings.truth: Heschel's own wording in The Sabbath (1951) is 'The Sabbaths are our great cathedrals' and 'a palace in time'. 'Cathedral in time' is a widespread paraphrase, not a verbatim quotation. Could not confirm the exact page text within the fetch budget, so recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Abraham Joshua Heschel (article does not quote the phrase); the book text was not reachable

findings.claim: examiners want you to go beyond description and explain the religious significance of each attribute
findings.truth: An unevidenced claim about what examiners want. The spec sets assessment objectives, not examiner preferences. Rewrite as a direct instruction to the student.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 assessment objectives (AO1 knowledge and understanding, AO2 analysis and evaluation); no examiner-report source

findings.claim: The ner tamid has never been extinguished since it was first lit.
findings.truth: False. There is no single continuous flame. Synagogues are built, closed and destroyed, and each community's ner tamid is its own lamp. Modern synagogue lamps are usually electric. The lamp is kept alight continuously; it is not one unbroken flame across history.
findings.evidence: spec practices list names ner tamid as a synagogue feature only; the historical claim is invented

findings.claim: examiners reward explanation of the religious reasons behind a practice, not just a description of what Jews do
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. Rewrite as a direct instruction.
findings.evidence: no examiner-report or mark-scheme source; spec assessment objectives only

findings.claim: The main rules of kashrut are drawn from Leviticus 11:1–24
findings.truth: The spec cites Leviticus 11:1-23 for the dietary laws. Verse 24 begins the separate section on uncleanness from carcasses. One verse out, not mark-affecting; the same citation appears in the conclusion, the exam tip and a knowledge-check option, so any change should be made in all four places together.
findings.evidence: spec line 3220 'requirements of a kosher kitchen: Leviticus 11:1-23'

findings.claim: They cover duties to G-d (no other gods, no images, Sabbath observance, honouring the divine name) and duties to other people (honouring parents, prohibitions on murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting).
findings.truth: This is the Christian grouping, not the Jewish one. In the Jewish enumeration 'Honour your father and your mother' is the fifth commandment and sits on the first tablet, with the duties to G-d, because honouring parents is treated as honouring G-d. The Jewish division is five and five: (1) 'I am the LORD your God', (2) no other gods or images, (3) not misusing the divine name, (4) Shabbat, (5) honouring parents; then murder, adultery, theft, false witness, coveting. Teaching the wrong division in a Judaism paper is a doctrinal error on named spec content.
findings.evidence: Jewish Virtual Library, The Ten Commandments (honour thy father and thy mother = fifth); Wikipedia, Ten Commandments (Talmudic enumeration; Rabbi Hanina ben Gamaliel, five per tablet); spec line 3186 lists the Ten Commandments as required content

findings.claim: Different Jewish movements hold different views on the Tenakh’s origin: Orthodox Jews regard it as the direct, verbatim word of G-d dictated to Moses
findings.truth: Orthodox Judaism holds that the Torah was given word for word to Moses (Torah min haShamayim). It does not hold that Nevi'im and Ketuvim were dictated to Moses; those are prophecy and inspired writing from later centuries. The claim is only true of the Torah.
findings.evidence: settled doctrine; the lesson's own earlier sentence already distinguishes Torah from the other two sections

findings.claim: examiners want more than a description of what happens — they want you to explain the religious reasons behind the practice
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. Rewrite as a direct instruction.

findings.claim: For bar/bat mitzvah, explain why the age of 13 is significant (it marks the point at which a Jew becomes personally responsible for the commandments).
findings.truth: 13 is the age for boys and for Reform girls. Orthodox girls become bat mitzvah at 12. The spec requires Orthodox and Reform views on Bat Mitzvah and Bat Chayil, so a flat 'age of 13' for bar and bat mitzvah together is wrong on examined content. The lesson body already says 'girls at 12 or 13'; the tip contradicts it.
findings.evidence: spec line 3211 'Orthodox and Reform views regarding Bat Mitzvah and Bat Chayil'; settled practice (Orthodox girls 12, boys 13)

findings.claim: It was established by the Israeli parliament (Knesset) in 1953
findings.truth: The Knesset set Yom HaShoah in law in 1959, by the Martyrs' and Heroes' Remembrance Day Law passed on 8 April 1959 and signed by David Ben-Gurion. The date of 27 Nisan had been fixed by a Knesset resolution in 1951. 1953 is the year of the Yad Vashem Law, not of the remembrance day.

'Lo Yishaney' is not Hebrew for 'never again' and is not a phrase used at Yom HaShoah. The Hebrew is 'le'olam lo od'. The transliteration is invented, so it should be deleted rather than replaced; the English phrase on its own is correct.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Yom HaShoah (no such phrase); the transliteration matches no standard Hebrew slogan

findings.claim: It is blown in a sequence of notes that include a long wailing sound (tekiah gedolah)
findings.truth: The tekiah gedolah is one very long unbroken blast, the 'great tekiah'. The broken and wailing sounds are shevarim (three broken notes) and teruah (short staccato notes). The lesson attaches the wrong sound to the named term.
findings.evidence: standard shofar terminology; Wikipedia, Shofar and Rosh Hashanah (blast sequence tekiah-shevarim-teruah-tekiah, with tekiah gedolah as the closing long blast)

findings.claim: The unit's festival lesson covers Yom Hashoah, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Pesach. Yom Hashoah has a full section and heads the lesson description.
findings.truth: The spec's festival list for this option is Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Pesach (Exodus 12:14), Sukkot, plus diversity of practice between Jewish traditions. Sukkot is required and is missing from the whole unit. Yom Hashoah is not on the list. Options: (a) leave Yom Hashoah as background and add a Sukkot section, which needs a content pass rather than a surgical edit; (b) replace the Yom Hashoah section with Sukkot; (c) leave as is and accept the gap. Purim is also absent, but the spec does not name it either, so only Sukkot is a true gap.
findings.evidence: spec lines 3222-3229 (Festivals: Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Pesach: Exodus 12:14, Sukkot, Diversity of practice)
findings.ruling: Leave: Sukkot section is a content-pass build item.

summary: Fourteen findings across four lessons: three HIGH (an invented history for the ner tamid, the Ten Commandments split in the Christian rather than the Jewish five-and-five division, and an invented Hebrew transliteration for 'Never Again'), eight MEDIUM and three LOW, giving ten surgical edits. Exam claims are otherwise sound: every practice question uses the 2/5/8/15 mark pattern of this paper, no lesson names the board, no lesson claims SPaG marks, and all twenty knowledge-check keys are correct. The one ADJUDICATE item is coverage: Sukkot is on the spec and absent from the unit, while an off-spec festival, Yom Hashoah, holds a full section.
